title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
official_title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
summary: Under current law, gasoline blended with 15% ethanol (E15) cannot be sold at gas stations during the high ozone season because E15 evaporates more readily than E10, contributing to ground-level ozone. This bill removes that seasonal ban by extending the existing E10 vapor pressure waiver to cover E15 year-round, allowing gas stations in all states to sell E15 during the summer high ozone season.
brief: Allows E15 ethanol-blended gasoline to be sold year-round by extending the E10 Reid Vapor Pressure waiver to E15, removing the current summer ozone-season prohibition.

top_lines.headline: Ethanol Blend Waiver
subs: Applies the existing Clean Air Act Reid Vapor Pressure waiver for E10 to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol
Removes the current high-ozone-season prohibition on E15 sales that applies in most of the country

top_lines.headline: Who It Affects
subs: Fuel retailers who currently stock separate summer and year-round fuel blends would be able to carry E15 year-round
Consumers in corn-belt states where E15 is already common would no longer face seasonal supply interruptions

likelihoodReason: Passed the House with 54 bipartisan cosponsors, signaling strong rural-state support. The Senate has passed similar measures before. However, opposition from oil refiners and some environmental groups over ozone concerns remains, and no Senate companion bill has advanced. Senate leadership is currently focused on the budget reconciliation process, limiting floor time for standalone bills.

items.main: Names the Act the “Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025.”
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act

items.main: Amends Section 211(h) of the Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7545(h)) to extend the Reid Vapor Pressure ethanol waiver from gasoline with 10 percent ethanol to blends of 10 to 15 percent ethanol.
items.detail: Restructures the Section 211(f)(4) waiver provision (42 U.S.C. 7545(f)(4)) and applies the paragraph (4) RVP limitation to all 10-to-15-percent denatured anhydrous ethanol blends sold during the high ozone season, including in States whose Governor's notification was submitted before enactment. Also amends Section 211(o)(9) (42 U.S.C. 7545(o)(9)) to allow certain small refineries to recover renewable-fuel credits retired for the 2016, 2017, and 2018 compliance years, either returned for future use or applied in the EPA Moderated Transaction System (EMTS) account.

underreported.summary: The RVP waiver extension applies to all ethanol blend percentages from 10% up to 15%, not just to E15 specifically. A retailer blending at 12% or 13% ethanol would also fall under the waiver.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title and sponsor statements focus on E15, but the statutory amendment covers any blend of 10 to 15 percent denatured anhydrous ethanol, meaning mid-range blends sold during the summer ozone season would also be exempt from the Clean Air Act §211(h) Reid Vapor Pressure limitation.

gaps: The bill removes the summer RVP restriction on E15 but does not address the separate infrastructure requirements — many fuel pumps and storage tanks require upgrades to handle E15 — that limit its availability regardless of the waiver.
The bill extends the waiver nationally but does not address California, which operates under a separate state waiver system and would require additional EPA approval to participate.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Budzinski
featured_quotes.text: As a lead Democrat on this bill, I have been proud to work with Congressman Adrian Smith on this issue. We both understand, like many other Members, that year-round E15 is bigger than politics. This is about American farmers. It is about American consumers, and it is about American energy. E15 is truly one of those rare issues where everyone wins. Here is why: American farmers win because it creates strong and stable markets for homegrown corn. American consumers win because E15 helps to lower prices at the pump.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Roy
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate my colleagues on both sides of this debate and where they are coming from. I understand my friends who come from States that want support for farming. We all want to make sure that we are figuring that out. We worked through the farm bill. I just think we ought to be going about this a different way. If we need to do something to support farmers, let's have a direct conversation about it. Expanding E15 is just the wrong direction to go. It is going to harm refiners. It is going to drive up the cost of gas.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: I rise to express my strong opposition to H.R. 1346. This bill is disastrous for Wyoming refiners and independent petroleum producers, leading to a direct loss of at least 750 jobs in my home State. Just to correct the record, it isn't the farmers who produce ethanol or E15. It is the refiners, and this bill threatens to put them out of business. In fact, it is interesting that anyone who supports this bill has not yet mentioned the fact that it is the refiners that will be forced, mandated, to meet the E15 requirement.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Finstad
featured_quotes.text: As a fourth-generation corn and soybean farmer from southern Minnesota raising that fifth generation and representing 21 counties in southern Minnesota, a very strong egg-producing district, I have had many conversations with my neighbor farmers. I know by hearing what they are telling me and firsthand in my own experience as a farmer that we are facing uncertainty in our input costs and uncertainty in the global markets. We need a new domestic opportunity for our corn. E15 delivers on that.

modified: Clean Air Act Section 211(h) — Reid Vapor Pressure waiver extended from gasoline blended with 10% ethanol to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol
removed: Seasonal prohibition on selling E15 during the high ozone season in non-waiver areas

added: New "small refining company" definition: daily average aggregate obligated-fuel production for calendar year 2025 not exceeding 75,000 barrels per day

Termination of small-refinery exemptions: beginning calendar year 2028 the Administrator may not extend exemptions; no petitions for years after 2027; petitions submitted after July 1, 2028 not considered; act on outstanding petitions by October 1, 2028
Adjusted compliance: beginning 2028, reduce each small refining company's RFS compliance requirements by 75 percent, with a no-subsequent-redesignation rule if production exceeds the limit
Prohibition on reallocating exempted small-refining-company renewable fuel obligations to others for 2028 onward
EPA fuel-infrastructure rulemaking within 18 months covering E15 dispenser labeling and underground storage tank compatibility for blends over 10% up to 15% ethanol

At-risk small refinery exemption (imminent closure/idling/conversion) with public-disclosure, 90-day action deadline, and a volume cap equal to 150 million gallons of conventional biofuel energy content for 2028
Savings provision preserving pre-enactment remedies for small refineries' extension petitions
modified: Short title "Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025" replaced; cross-references in the RVP amendments now cite the "Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026"
Section heading changed from "Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act" to "Year-Round E15 and RFS Reform"
State RVP retroactivity narrowed to notifications submitted after January 1, 2022 and before enactment (was simply before enactment)
